definition.text: The branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it.

facts.text: It emerged as a branch of philosophy in the 1970s; early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott.
A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only instrumental value, with ecocentric and deep ecology views against human-centred ones.
Current issues include environmental activism, environmental justice, climate change and the depletion of finite resources.
Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists or is a cultural construct with colonial overtones, as William Cronon suggested.
Its questions include whether rivers have rights.

definition.text: The ways societies see importance in the non-human world, grouped as extrinsic (instrumental), intrinsic and relational values.

facts.text: Extrinsic values are nature's usefulness to people, such as timber, clean water and air, carbon storage and pollination, often called ecosystem services.
Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value and so enter impact assessments, cost-benefit analyses and national accounts.
Intrinsic values hold that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans.
Relational values are the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.
IPBES, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

definition.text: Murray Bookchin's 1982 philosophy linking how humans treat nature to how they treat each other.

facts.text: It defines nature as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom.
Bookchin argued that 'the ecological crisis is a social crisis': practices such as monocropping and overfishing mirror social tendencies to dominate people.
It calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

definition.text: In political economy, especially Marxian economics, the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods.

facts.text: It is one of four attributes of a commodity, alongside use value, value and price.
For Marx, exchange value is not the same as money price; actual prices only roughly match it.
Marx held that a good's value is set by the socially necessary labour time needed to produce it.
Making something a commodity requires preconditions such as secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand.
Modern neoclassical economics no longer theorises exchange value separately; it is simply the market price.
Critics of the commodification of nature argue that expressing all kinds of worth through a single exchange value makes things commensurable.

definition.text: The value people place on a good, often a natural resource, even if they never have used it and never will.

facts.text: It is distinguished from use value, which comes from using the good directly.
It can include option value, bequest value, existence value and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it.
All these categories grew from the idea of option value introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964.
Because market prices and other revealed preference methods generally cannot measure it, stated preference surveys such as contingent valuation are used.
Ecosystem valuation sorts the value of ecosystem services into use and non-use categories.

definition.text: The puzzle, also called the diamond–water paradox, that water is far more useful for survival than diamonds, yet diamonds cost much more.

facts.text: Adam Smith is its classic presenter, though it appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus.
Smith separated 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', noting that the most useful things often have little exchange value.
Labor theory of value supporters resolve it by saying price reflects the toil of acquiring a good.
Marginalists resolve it by distinguishing total from marginal utility: water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more.
Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons.
A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.
